html:
On 3 March 1924 the Grand National Assembly of Turkey abolished the Ottoman caliphate, the last caliphate widely recognised in the Sunni Muslim world. The last caliph, Abdulmejid II, and the rest of the Ottoman family were sent into exile.

The caliph was in theory the successor of Muhammad as leader of all Muslims. The office had passed from the early caliphs through the Abbasids, and the Ottoman sultans claimed it from the 16th century. When the sultanate ended in 1922, the caliphate was kept as a religious office, but Mustafa Kemal saw it as a rallying point for his opponents.

The decision shocked Muslims elsewhere, above all in British India, where the Khilafat movement had campaigned to save it. Attempts to revive a caliphate in Cairo and Mecca failed. The idea lived on in Islamist thought, from the Muslim Brotherhood to the group that declared a caliphate in 2014.
sum: On 3 March 1924 the Grand National Assembly of Turkey abolished the Ottoman caliphate, the last caliphate widely recognised in the Sunni Muslim world. The last caliph, Abdulmejid II, and the rest of the Ottoman family were sent into exile.
